A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SPQR benchmark. All main-text and appendix pages, including equations, tables and figures, support comparison despite retitling, substantial reformatting and additional experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original safety and utility experiments across alignment methods, benign fine-tuning profiles, languages, domains and backbones, including appendix LoRA-rank ablations.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds human validation, SD3 and FLUX results, sensitivity analyses and a safety-recovery experiment.

M1.justification: The same existing alignment methods and full-parameter, cross-attention and LoRA adaptation procedures remain. The recovery experiment reapplies existing alignment methods. Revisions to SPQR normalization and aggregation concern evaluation definitions, rather than a new alignment algorithm or model.

E1.justification: Both retain COCO, Arabic/French/Spanish/Hindi adaptations, artistic and medical data, and ViSU, I2P and Ring-A-Bell evaluations. The human audit uses an in-distribution subset of existing categories. Additional backbones and re-alignment procedures change experimental settings without expanding the represented data or domains.

E2.justification: The SD2.1 benchmark comparison narrows from AdvUnlearn, ESD, SPM and UCE in v1 Table D to ESD and UCE in v2 Table 11. AdvUnlearn and SPM remain in the separate LoRA-rank experiment. The eleven-method SD1.5 comparison and four-method SDXL comparison are retained.

E3.justification: Section 3.3 changes prompt adherence from raw CLIPScore to normalization against an unaligned SD3 reference. V2 adds SD3/FLUX configurations, a 250-image audit with three annotators and majority voting, learning-rate and aggregation variants, and post-BFT re-alignment. Existing base hyperparameters and BFT profiles remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds human validation of the safety classifiers (Table 1), learning-rate sensitivity (Figure 6), normalization/weight/temperature sensitivity (Table 10), and reversibility of safety degradation (Table 13). These test measurement validity, calibration dependence and recovery. The profile, domain, harmful-prompt and LoRA-rank analyses already existed in v1.

E5.justification: V2 newly reports Spearman rank correlations against the default ranking for nine aggregation variants in Table 10. This adds a statistical ranking-stability summary. Both versions retain seed 42; v2 does not introduce confidence intervals, significance tests or documented additional repeated runs.

E6.justification: Rescoring changes many reported values: RECE's SD1.5 general prompt-adherence/SPQR values change from 0.292/0.608 to 0.973/0.956, reflecting normalization rather than demonstrated performance gains. V2 also adds SD3/FLUX results, human-validation macro F1 of 0.87, sensitivity findings, and safety recovery of 86%, 81% and 60% for RECE, ESD and FMN.

T1.justification: V2 defines SD3-normalized prompt adherence, generalizes Equation 7 with axis weights, and introduces temperature-dependent robustness in Appendix B.3. These are limited mathematical extensions of the existing scoring framework. The threat-model equations remain unchanged, and neither version supplies formal proofs.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the unintentional-attacker threat model, four-axis SPQR evaluation, and evidence that benign adaptation can undermine safety while preserving utility. The adaptation-dependent failure claim also remains. Added validation and backbone experiments support these existing claims without redefining the core contribution.

C2.justification: Appendix A.1 newly distinguishes the BFT threat from auxiliary adversarial stress tests and cautions against optimizing the scalar score alone because of detector overfitting. New sections interpret sensitivity and partial recovery as evidence about structural safety, while explicitly qualifying the recovery study as preliminary. Existing limitations largely remain.

D1.justification: V2 provides a project-code URL, documents the human-annotation procedure and new sensitivity configurations, and explains the smoothing constant with an example value. The optimizer, base learning rate, batch size, resolution and LoRA configuration tables are retained. The PDFs alone do not verify the linked code's availability.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations for LLaVA-Guard, CLIPScore, FID and two recent unlearning/safety-drift works. The SDXL technical-report citation disappears with the removed backbone-history discussion. The main method taxonomy and positioning against existing benchmarks remain; the STEREO publication update represents the same work.

P1.justification: V2 retitles the paper, edits the introduction and conclusion, standardizes BFT/scenario terminology, adds appendix navigation and subsections, and replaces the Stable Diffusion history with focused backbone results. Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain recognizable.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout, substantially altering figure sizes and float placement. Backbone comparisons are regrouped, with SDXL moved into the main benchmark table. Human-validation, aggregation-sensitivity and recovery tables and a learning-rate figure are added; existing qualitative and radar figures are largely retained.

improvement.justification: Human validation, sensitivity checks, DiT-backbone results and code-access information strengthen evidence and transparency beyond v1. However, the scoring revision is incompletely propagated: Section 4.4 still reports RECE's old 0.608 score while Table 2 gives 0.956. Appendix B.2 also calls the default learning rate a mid-range choice although Table 8 places it at the tested upper endpoint. These inconsistencies limit the overall gain.
